source.title: Scaling Beyond Masked Diffusion Language Models
source.authors: S. Sahoo; Jean-Marie Lemercier; Zhi-Han Yang; Justin Deschenaux; Jingyu Liu; John Thickstun; Ante Jukic

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including the appendix, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses compute-matched IsoFLOP sweeps and validation-loss scaling fits to examine scaling behavior, including an autoregressive reference and several diffusion model families.
record.gate_note: The scaling sweeps and compute-optimal model-size results are recorded below. The 1.7B downstream benchmark and SFT results do not measure downstream performance across scale or its relation to pretraining loss; sampling throughput and generated-sample quality are also outside the listed versions. Results cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study runs Hoffmann-style IsoFLOP sweeps (5 budgets, 6e18–1e20 FLOPs) on SlimPajama. It fits power laws for compute-optimal validation loss and parameter count against compute. The AR reference reproduces the familiar behaviour, and the main new setting is three discrete-diffusion language model families. Its own results bear on V1, V3 (parameter-count part) and V7 (training objective shifts the compute-optimal size).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that diffusion LMs show scaling exponents comparable to AR with large family-dependent constant-factor gaps; MDLM has the strongest likelihood scaling. A low-variance objective improves MDLM compute efficiency by about 12% and yields smaller compute-optimal models. Perplexity is informative within a family but misleading across families: Duo and Eso-LM can dominate the speed-quality frontier, and Duo beats AR on GSM8K after SFT at 1.7B.
record.recipe_differences: Uses compute-matched IsoFLOP sweeps and compute-optimal scaling fits, but applies them to discrete diffusion families as well as an AR reference; it uses exact FLOP accounting, SlimPajama, a fixed tokenizer and context length, and the tested diffusion-specific objectives.
record.method_sensitivity: The MDLM training objective changes compute efficiency and the compute-optimal model size: the low-variance objective reduces the reported compute multiplier to match AR validation loss from ≈ 16× to ≈ 14× and shifts optimal checkpoints toward smaller models.

fits_no_version.finding: Diffusion families scale with exponents comparable to AR but need about 14–32× more compute to match AR loss. The constant factor depends on family and objective (MDLM 16×→14× with the low-variance loss; Duo 23×; Eso-LM 32×).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across generative objectives for text, loss–compute exponents are similar while constant-factor compute gaps differ widely.

fits_no_version.finding: At 1.7B, Duo has worse validation perplexity than AR and MDLM but the best GSM8K accuracy after SFT (65.8 vs AR 62.9). Perplexity is called misleading across diffusion families.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining loss does not predict downstream performance across model families with different likelihood bounds.

record.problems: The scaling study uses five compute budgets from 6 × 10^18 to 1 × 10^20 and reports no numerical fitted exponents or uncertainty estimates in the text. The study does not validate extrapolation to runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitting runs.
record.rows_left_out: None of the reported scaling results within the 60-row limit were left out.

untested.parts: Loss power laws in parameters or tokens separately with the other quantities non-bottleneck. Validity over several orders of magnitude: the compute range spans under 1.5 orders (6e18–1e20).
No extrapolation test: the 1.7B models' loss is not compared with predictions from the fits.
No compute-optimal token-count fit, and no test of the Kaplan vs Hoffmann split (whether N grows faster than or equally with D). No fitted exponent γ is reported.
Not tested. Shapes vary with size (Table 4), but there is no fixed-N comparison.
Not tested. All scaling runs are text pretraining.
Not tested across scale. Downstream results come only at 1.7B.

Fitting method, parameter-counting conventions and schedule/data variation are not compared. Exact calflops FLOP counting is used instead of 6ND, but the two are not contrasted. Bending away from a power law is not examined.

missing.what: Fractional compute-optimal size difference of low-variance MDLM vs ELBO MDLM, about 0 to −15% across budgets
Fitted exponents α* and γ are never given numerically. Only the figures and the word 'comparable' support exponent similarity across families.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The tranche is T3 because the main contribution is the diffusion-LM setting; the AR reference reproduces the IsoFLOP method (T1-like). The V7 label was changed from limits_scope to supports, since objective-dependence of the compute-optimal size is what V7 asserts. The compute range is narrow (under 1.5 orders of magnitude), no uncertainty is reported, and five budgets is a small number of points.

versions.untested_parts: The study fits compute-optimal validation loss against training compute. It does not separately establish loss power laws against parameter count or token count with the other quantities non-bottleneck.
No explicit prediction from small-run fits is compared with the loss of runs orders of magnitude larger.
The study fits compute-optimal parameter count against compute, but does not report a fitted compute-optimal token-count trend or test whether parameter count grows faster or equally to token count.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The scaling study is of text pretraining. SFT is reported at a fixed model size, not as a scaling-law test.
Downstream benchmark scores are reported at a fixed model size; the study does not test their relationship to scale or pretraining loss.

The study shows that changing MDLM's training objective changes compute efficiency and compute-optimal model size. It does not compare fitting methods or parameter-count conventions, test whether curves bend away from a single power law, or comprehensively vary data and training schedules.
